Section 2 • Cosmological Background and Photon Trajectories

2.3 Evolution of the scale factor along the line of sight

It is often more convenient to characterize the photon trajectory by the scale factor \(a\) as a function of comoving position \(x\), rather than by \(x(t)\) itself. In particular, our absorption formalism will require us to evaluate relative photon wavelength along the line of sight while keeping track of the cosmological epoch associated with each point.

Using \(\dot a = aH(a)\), together with Eq. (2.3), the chain rule gives \begin{equation} \frac{da}{dx} = \frac{da}{dt} \frac{dt}{dx} = \pm \frac{a^2H(a)}{\cc\sqrt{1-\kappa x^2}}. \tag{2.4} \end{equation} Choose the lower (\(-\)) sign for a past-directed ray received “today” (so \(a\) decreases as \(x\) increases); choose the upper (\(+\)) sign for future-directed rays.

Substituting Eq. (2.2) into Eq. (2.4), we obtain \begin{equation} \frac{da}{dx} = \pm \frac{H_0}{\cc} \sqrt{ \frac{ \Omega_r + \Omega_m a + \Omega_k a^2 + \Omega_\Lambda a^4 }{ 1-\kappa x^2 } }. \tag{2.5} \end{equation}

This is the form that will be most useful later on: once a photon path is parametrized by the comoving coordinate \(x\), Eq. (2.5) specifies which scale factor, and therefore which redshift, corresponds to each point along the line of sight.

Interactive

2.3.1 Some Analytic Solutions

In simple Limiting cases, Eq. 2.5 can be integrated analytically. These examples are useful to build intuition and to check the consistency of numerical implementations. They show explicitly how the scale factor varies along the photon trajectory when a single component dominates the expansion.

For example for matter domination: \begin{align} \int_{a_0}^{a}\frac{da}{\sqrt{a}} = \frac{H_0}{c}\int_{x_0}^{x} dx \longrightarrow a(x) = \left( a_0^{1/2} + \frac{H_0}{2c}\left(x - x_0\right)\right)^2 \tag{2.6} \end{align}

For radiation domination \begin{align} \int_{a_0}^{a}da = \frac{H_0}{c}\int_{x_0}^{x} dx \longrightarrow a(x) = a_0 + \frac{H_0}{c}\left(x - x_0\right) \tag{2.7} \end{align}

These analytic expressions are not meant to describe the full late-time cosmology, but rather to illustrate the structure of the solution in simple regimes. In more realistic situations, several components contribute simultaneously to \(H(a)\), and the resulting equation is typically solved numerically. See Appendix A for a brief discussion regarding how to numerically solve systems of ODEs such as Equation 2.5. Figure 1 illustrates how some of these numerical solutions compare to the analytical ones.
